title: Streaming & Change Data Capture
summary: How change data capture turns a database's write-ahead log into an event stream, why windows must use event time with watermarks for out-of-order data, and how commit-after-processing plus idempotent writes gives effectively-once results across crashes.
takeaways: CDC reads committed changes from the database log in order. The LSN tells you what you've already applied.
Window by event time, not processing time. Watermarks decide when a window is complete, and late data is handled explicitly.
Commit offsets after processing (at-least-once). Committing before processing loses data on a crash.
At-least-once delivery plus idempotent or deduplicated writes gives effectively-once results.

steps.label: Poll
steps.detail: Read the next records from the last committed offset.

steps.label: Deduplicate
steps.detail: Skip records whose id (or LSN) has already been applied.

steps.label: Process + write
steps.detail: Update the sink, and record the id in the same atomic write.

steps.label: Commit offset
steps.detail: Only now advance the committed offset past the batch.

steps.label: Crash? Restart
steps.detail: Resume from the last commit. Redelivered records are harmless duplicates.

terms.definition: Streaming every committed insert, update and delete from a database, usually by reading its write-ahead log.
Log sequence number: a position in the write-ahead log that increases with commit order.
When an event happened, versus when the system happens to process it.
The system's estimate that no events older than time t are still to come. It closes event-time windows.
Extra time a window stays open after the watermark passes its end, so stragglers still count.
Durably recording how far a consumer has read in a partition, so a restart resumes there.
